label: فصل ۱
title: معرفت‌شناسی چیست؟
q: هر یک را در یکی از سه دستهٔ معرفتِ گزاره‌ای، دانستنِ چگونگی یا معرفت از راهِ آشنایی بگذارید: (الف) علی بوی باران روی خاکِ خشک را می‌شناسد. (ب) علی می‌داند که بوی خاکِ باران‌خورده تا اندازه‌ای از روغن‌های گیاهی و ژئوسمین است. (ج) علی می‌داند چگونه از رنگِ آسمان باران را پیش‌بینی کند.
a: (الف) آشنایی. (ب) گزاره‌ای. (ج) دانستنِ چگونگی. بنا بر دیدگاهِ عقل‌گرایانه، (ج) شاید به معرفتِ گزاره‌ای به شیوه‌ای برای پیش‌بینیِ باران فروکاسته شود، و می‌توان استدلال کرد که (الف) هم معرفتِ گزاره‌ای را در بر دارد. این دسته‌ها نقطهٔ آغازند، نه نظریه‌ای نهایی.

label: فصل ۱
title: معرفت‌شناسی چیست؟
q: «همهٔ روباه‌های ماده روباه‌اند و ماده‌اند» را بر پایهٔ سه تمایز دسته‌بندی کنید.
a: پیشین (با فهمیدنِ واژه‌ها دانستنی است)، تحلیلی (به‌خاطرِ معنا صادق است)، ضروری (نمی‌تواند کاذب باشد). این نمونهٔ معیاری است که هر سه در آن بر هم منطبق‌اند.

label: فصل ۱
title: معرفت‌شناسی چیست؟
q: چرا «آب H₂O است» از نظرِ فلسفی جالب است؟
a: کریپکی استدلال کرد که این گزاره ضروری است (در هر جهانِ ممکنی آب H₂O است، چون آب همین است) اما فقط پسین دانسته می‌شود (از راهِ شیمی). این فرضِ قدیمی را می‌شکند که همهٔ صدق‌های ضروری پیشین دانسته می‌شوند.

label: فصل ۱
title: معرفت‌شناسی چیست؟
q: دوستی می‌گوید: «به طلسمِ شانس باور دارم چون پیش از امتحان آرامم می‌کند.» این چه نوع دلیلی است، و اشکالش چیست؟
a: دلیلی عملی است: به فایده‌های داشتنِ باور مربوط است، نه به شاهدی بر خوش‌یُمن بودنِ طلسم. دوستتان شاید «باور به اینکه طلسم کار می‌کند» را با «همراه داشتنِ طلسم آرام‌بخش است» اشتباه می‌گیرد. اثرِ آرام‌بخش می‌تواند واقعی باشد (باور ممکن است مثلِ دارونما عمل کند) حتی اگر طلسم هیچ نیروی علّی بر نتیجهٔ امتحان نداشته باشد. این نمونهٔ خوبی است از اینکه چرا تمایزِ عملی و معرفتی مهم است.

label: فصل ۱
title: معرفت‌شناسی چیست؟
q: تفاوتِ باور داشتن به یک گزاره و پذیرفتنِ آن چیست؟ مثالی از علم بزنید.
a: باور داشتن به p یعنی p را صادق دانستن. پذیرفتنِ p یعنی آن را در زمینه‌ای معین مقدمهٔ استدلال یا عمل قرار دادن، چه به آن باور داشته باشید چه نه. فیزیک‌دان هنگامِ محاسبهٔ مدارِ سیاره‌ای می‌پذیرد که سیاره جرمی نقطه‌ای است، با اینکه می‌داند سیاره‌ها جرمِ نقطه‌ای نیستند.

label: فصل ۱
title: معرفت‌شناسی چیست؟
q: دو فرمانِ ویلیام جیمز را توضیح دهید و بگویید چرا با هم تعارض دارند.
a: «به حقیقت باور کن!» و «از خطا بپرهیز!». اگر اولی را بیشینه کنید، باید تا جای ممکن باور کنید تا هیچ صدقی از دستتان نرود، و در این میان بسیاری کذب‌ها را هم خواهید گرفت. اگر دومی را بیشینه کنید، باید به هیچ چیز باور نکنید تا از هر خطایی دور بمانید، و در این میان همهٔ صدق‌ها را هم از دست خواهید داد. باورِ عقلانی مستلزمِ ایجادِ توازن میانِ این دو است. این توازن می‌تواند به‌حق با زمینه جابه‌جا شود، مثلاً با هزینهٔ خطاها.

label: فصل ۱
title: معرفت‌شناسی چیست؟
q: در گفت‌وگوی سرِ سفرهٔ آغازِ این فصل، «ب» می‌گوید «حکایت‌های شخصی شاهد نیستند». آیا «ب» درست می‌گوید؟
a: نه کاملاً. یک حکایتِ شخصی به معنای احتمالاتی شاهد است، چون کاهشِ وزنِ پسرعمه اگر رژیم کار کند کمی محتمل‌تر است تا اگر کار نکند. اما شاهدی بسیار ضعیف است. یک مورد است، گروهِ کنترل ندارد، ممکن است حاصلِ گزینش باشد (خبرِ موفقیت‌ها به گوشمان می‌رسد)، و علت‌های دیگری می‌توانند آن را توضیح دهند. بیانِ بهتر: «یک حکایتِ شخصی بسیار ضعیف‌تر از آن است که نشان دهد رژیم کار می‌کند.»

label: فصل ۲
title: تاریخِ نظریهٔ معرفت
q: پارادوکسِ منون چیست، و چرا هنوز معمایی واقعی است؟
a: اگر ندانید دنبالِ چه می‌گردید، وقتی پیدایش کنید بازش نمی‌شناسید؛ اگر بدانید، نیازی به گشتن ندارید. پس پژوهش ناممکن به نظر می‌رسد. این همچنان معماست چون پژوهشِ واقعی با معرفتِ ناقص کار می‌کند: به‌قدرِ کافی می‌دانیم تا پرسشی را صورت‌بندی کنیم و پاسخی خوب را بازشناسیم، بی‌آنکه از پیش پاسخ را بدانیم. توضیحِ اینکه این معرفتِ ناقص چگونه کشف را هدایت می‌کند مسئله‌ای واقعی در معرفت‌شناسی و فلسفهٔ علم است.

label: فصل ۲
title: تاریخِ نظریهٔ معرفت
q: مثالِ هیئتِ منصفه در تئایتتوس را بیان کنید. چه چیزی را نشان می‌دهد؟
a: سخنوری زبردست هیئتِ منصفه را به حکمی درست دربارهٔ رویدادهایی قانع می‌کند که فقط شاهدی عینی می‌توانست بداند. اعضای هیئت به باورِ صادق می‌رسند اما نه به معرفت، چون باورشان بر اقناع استوار است نه بر پایه‌های خوب. این نشان می‌دهد که باورِ صادق برای معرفت کافی نیست.

label: فصل ۲
title: تاریخِ نظریهٔ معرفت
q: چنگالِ هیوم را توضیح دهید و با آن مسئلهٔ استقرای او را بازسازی کنید.
a: چنگالِ هیوم: هر استدلالی یا دربارهٔ نسبت‌های میانِ ایده‌هاست (پیشین، یقینی، انکارش متناقض) یا دربارهٔ امورِ واقع (دانسته با تجربه، انکارش تصورپذیر). استقرا فرض می‌کند که آینده به گذشته شبیه خواهد بود (اصلِ یکنواختی). این اصل نسبتی میانِ ایده‌ها نیست، چون انکارش تصورپذیر است. با تجربه هم اثبات نمی‌شود، چون هر استدلالی از تجربه پیشاپیش آن را فرض می‌گیرد (دور). پس هیچ پشتیبانِ عقلانی ندارد، و استقرا هم ندارد.

label: فصل ۲
title: تاریخِ نظریهٔ معرفت
q: استدلالِ هم‌ترازیِ رید در برابرِ شکاک چیست؟
a: شکاک به عقل اعتماد می‌کند اما به ادراک بی‌اعتماد است. رید یادآور می‌شود که هر دو قوه یک خاستگاه دارند («از یک کارگاه بیرون آمده‌اند»). اگر برای ادراک تضمینی مستقل نداریم، برای عقل هم نداریم. پس اعتمادِ گزینشیِ شکاک دلبخواهی است. یا به هر دو اعتماد کنید، چنان‌که رید توصیه می‌کند، یا به هر دو بی‌اعتماد باشید، که در این صورت استدلال‌های خودِ شکاک، که از عقل استفاده می‌کنند، خود را سست می‌کنند.

label: فصل ۲
title: تاریخِ نظریهٔ معرفت
q: چرا اصلِ تحقیق‌پذیریِ پوزیتیویسمِ منطقی شکست خورد؟
a: دلیلِ اصلی خودشکنی است: این اصل نه تحلیلی است و نه به‌طورِ تجربی تحقیق‌پذیر، پس بنا به معیارِ خودش بی‌معناست. دشواری‌های فنی هم وجود داشت: هر روایتِ دقیق یا گزاره‌های علمیِ واقعی را بیرون می‌گذاشت (قانون‌های کلی را نمی‌توان به‌طورِ قطعی تحقیق کرد) یا گزاره‌های متافیزیکی را راه می‌داد.

label: فصل ۲
title: تاریخِ نظریهٔ معرفت
q: کشتیِ نویرات تصویرِ چیست؟
a: تصویرِ این ایده که نمی‌توانیم از کلِ نظامِ باورهایمان بیرون برویم و آن را از پایه‌هایی تردیدناپذیر از نو بسازیم، چنان‌که دکارت امید داشت. باید باورها را تکه‌تکه تعمیر کنیم و در این میان به بقیه تکیه کنیم. این تصویر با انسجام‌گرایی و طبیعت‌گراییِ کواین پیوند دارد.

label: فصل ۲
title: تاریخِ نظریهٔ معرفت
q: سه اندیشمند را نام ببرید که کوگیتوی دکارت را پیش‌بینی کردند و سه اندیشمند که دیدگاهِ هیوم دربارهٔ علیت یا استقرا را پیش‌بینی کردند.
a: کوگیتو: آگوستین (si fallor, sum)، ابن سینا (انسانِ معلق در هوا)، و به یک معنا سهروردی (علمِ حضوریِ نفس به خود). علیت و استقرا: چارواکه (نقدِ استنتاج)، غزالی (پیوندِ ضروریِ مشاهده‌نشده) و نیکلاسِ اوترکوری.

label: فصل ۲
title: تاریخِ نظریهٔ معرفت
q: «بت‌های قبیله»ی بیکن را با سوگیریِ تأییدیِ امروزی مقایسه کنید.
a: بیکن گرایشِ ذهن را توصیف کرد که وقتی عقیده‌ای را پذیرفت، نمونه‌های پشتیبان را گرد می‌آورد و نمونه‌های مخالف را نادیده می‌گیرد یا توجیه می‌کند. روان‌شناسیِ امروز همین پدیده را سوگیریِ تأییدی (یا سوگیریِ جانب‌دارانه) می‌نامد و از دههٔ ۱۹۶۰ آن را به‌طورِ تجربی مستند کرده است (برای نمونه در کارِ واسون).

label: فصل ۳
title: منطق و کالبدشناسیِ استدلال
q: این استدلال است یا تبیین؟ «دایناسورها منقرض شدند چون ۶۶ میلیون سال پیش سیارکی به شبه‌جزیرهٔ یوکاتان خورد.»
a: معمولاً تبیین است: فرض می‌گیرد که دایناسورها منقرض شدند و می‌گوید چرا. در بحثی میانِ دیرین‌شناسان دربارهٔ اینکه آیا سیارک علت بوده است، همین جمله می‌تواند نتیجهٔ استدلالی باشد که شواهدی مانندِ لایهٔ ایریدیوم و دهانهٔ چیکشولوب از آن پشتیبانی می‌کنند.

label: فصل ۳
title: منطق و کالبدشناسیِ استدلال
q: معتبر یا نامعتبر؟ «اگر متهم در صحنه بود، اثرِ انگشتش روی تفنگ می‌بود. اثرِ انگشتش روی تفنگ است. پس در صحنه بود.»
a: نامعتبر. این وضعِ تالی است. اثرِ انگشت ممکن است به راه‌های دیگری آنجا رفته باشد (پیش‌تر تفنگ را در دست گرفته، یا کسی آن را کار گذاشته است). با این همه توجه کنید که اثرِ انگشت هنوز شاهدی بر حضورِ او در صحنه است. صورتِ قیاسی نامعتبر است، اما پشتیبانیِ استقرایی ممکن است قابل‌توجه باشد.

label: فصل ۳
title: منطق و کالبدشناسیِ استدلال
q: عکس، وارون و عکسِ نقیضِ این گزاره را بنویسید: «اگر عددی بر ۴ بخش‌پذیر باشد، زوج است.» کدام‌ها صادق‌اند؟
a: عکس: «اگر عددی زوج باشد، بر ۴ بخش‌پذیر است.» کاذب (۶). وارون: «اگر عددی بر ۴ بخش‌پذیر نباشد، زوج نیست.» کاذب (۶). عکسِ نقیض: «اگر عددی زوج نباشد، بر ۴ بخش‌پذیر نیست.» صادق، و هم‌ارزِ اصل.

label: فصل ۳
title: منطق و کالبدشناسیِ استدلال
q: «فقط اگر مدرکِ دانشگاهی داشته باشید می‌توانید شغلِ خوبی پیدا کنید.» آیا این یعنی داشتنِ مدرک شغلِ خوب را تضمین می‌کند؟
a: نه. «P فقط اگر Q» یعنی P → Q: داشتنِ مدرک برای شغلِ خوب لازم است، نه کافی. (اینکه آیا حتی ادعای لزوم صادق است پرسشی جداگانه است.)

label: فصل ۳
title: منطق و کالبدشناسیِ استدلال
q: مغالطهٔ صوری را بازشناسید: «همهٔ دانشمندانِ خوب شکاک‌اند. مارک شکاک است. پس مارک دانشمندِ خوبی است.»
a: حدِ وسطِ غیرمستغرق (یا به‌طورِ هم‌ارز، وضعِ تالی در صورتِ محمولی). بنا بر مقدمه، شکاک بودن برای دانشمندِ خوب بودن لازم است، نه کافی.

label: فصل ۳
title: منطق و کالبدشناسیِ استدلال
q: این استدلال چه اشکالی دارد: «هر کسی هدفی دارد، پس یک هدف هست که همه دارند»؟
a: جابه‌جاییِ سورها: از ∀x ∃y (y هدفِ x است) به ∃y ∀x (y هدفِ x است). هر کسی ممکن است هدفی متفاوت داشته باشد.

label: فصل ۳
title: منطق و کالبدشناسیِ استدلال
q: مقدمهٔ مفقود را فراهم و ارزیابی کنید: «معلوم است که آن مقاله غلط است. یک فعالِ محیط‌زیستیِ اقلیم نوشته‌اش.»
a: مقدمهٔ مفقود: «مقاله‌هایی که فعالانِ اقلیم می‌نویسند (همیشه یا معمولاً) غلط‌اند.» با این بیان، مقدمه آشکارا ناموجه است. این صورتی از مغالطهٔ حمله به شخص یا مغالطهٔ منشأ است. مقدمه‌ای منصفانه‌تر، «فعالان ممکن است انگیزه‌هایی داشته باشند که آنان را در دقت کم‌حوصله‌تر کند»، می‌تواند بررسیِ بیشترِ ادعاهای مقاله را موجه کند، اما نمی‌تواند نشان دهد مقاله غلط است. پاسخِ درست وارسیِ ادعاهاست.

label: فصل ۳
title: منطق و کالبدشناسیِ استدلال
q: این را در صورتِ تولمین بنویسید: «باید چتر برداریم؛ پیش‌بینیِ هوا می‌گوید ۸۰٪ احتمالِ باران هست.»
a: داده: پیش‌بینی ۸۰٪ احتمالِ باران می‌دهد. مجوز: وقتی باران محتمل است، برداشتنِ چتر عاقلانه است. پشتوانه: پیش‌بینی‌ها در این سطحِ اطمینان به‌طورِ معقولی کالیبره‌اند، و خیس شدن ناخوشایند است در حالی که چتر هزینهٔ کمی دارد. قید: احتمالاً. ادعا: باید چتر برداریم. ردیه: مگر آنکه تمامِ مدت داخلِ ساختمان باشیم، یا باد برای چتر بیش از حد تند باشد.

label: فصل ۳
title: منطق و کالبدشناسیِ استدلال
q: توضیح دهید چگونه یک استدلالِ واحد را هم شکاک و هم مخالفِ شکاکیت می‌تواند به کار ببرد.
a: اگر P → Q پذیرفته شود، شکاک با وضعِ مقدم از P به Q می‌رسد، و مخالفِ شکاکیت با رفعِ تالی از نقیضِ Q به نقیضِ P. شکاک: «اگر نتوانم خواب دیدن را منتفی کنم، نمی‌دانم دست دارم؛ نمی‌توانم منتفی‌اش کنم؛ پس نمی‌دانم.» مور: «اگر نتوانم خواب دیدن را منتفی کنم، نمی‌دانم دست دارم؛ می‌دانم دست دارم؛ پس (به نحوی) می‌توانم منتفی‌اش کنم.» منطق تعیین می‌کند که P و Q با هم بمانند یا با هم بیفتند؛ اطمینانِ نسبیِ ما تعیین می‌کند به کدام سو برویم.

label: فصل ۴
title: زبان، مفاهیم و تعریف‌ها
q: Identify the use/mention confusion: “‘Infinity’ is a word with eight letters, so infinity is finite.”
a: The premise is about the word “infinity” (mention); the conclusion is about infinity itself (use). The word’s finite length says nothing about the concept’s content.

label: فصل ۴
title: زبان، مفاهیم و تعریف‌ها
q: “The police are looking for the person who robbed the bank. I know that my neighbor is the kind of person who would never rob a bank. So the police are not looking for my neighbor.” What fallacy is this, and what’s wrong with it?
a: It is a relative of the masked man fallacy and involves an intensional context (“looking for”). The police are looking for whoever robbed the bank, under that description. If the neighbor did in fact rob the bank, the police are looking for the neighbor, whatever the speaker believes about the neighbor’s character. There is also a hidden inductive leap from character to action.

label: فصل ۴
title: زبان، مفاهیم و تعریف‌ها
q: What kind of definition is “Obesity means a body mass index of 30 or more”? What are its advantages and risks?
a: It is a precising definition that is also operational (defined by a measurement procedure). Advantages: clear, measurable, comparable across studies. Risks: BMI does not distinguish muscle from fat and varies in predictive value across populations. Conclusions about “obesity” in the BMI sense may not carry over to obesity in the medical sense of excess body fat that harms health. Goodhart’s law applies if BMI becomes a target.

label: فصل ۴
title: زبان، مفاهیم و تعریف‌ها
q: Find a counterexample to: “A chair is a piece of furniture with four legs that you sit on.”
a: Too narrow: three-legged stools and chairs with a single pedestal or runners. Too broad: a four-legged bench or sofa, or a four-legged table that someone sits on. “Chair” is probably a family-resemblance or prototype concept.

label: فصل ۴
title: زبان، مفاهیم و تعریف‌ها
q: Is this a verbal dispute? A: “Viruses are alive; they evolve and reproduce.” B: “Viruses are not alive; they have no metabolism and cannot reproduce on their own.”
a: Largely verbal. The parties agree on the facts (viruses evolve, reproduce only inside host cells, and lack their own metabolism) and disagree on whether “alive” requires metabolism and independent reproduction. Banning the word “alive” dissolves the factual disagreement. A substantive question may remain: which concept of life is most useful for biology?

label: فصل ۴
title: زبان، مفاهیم و تعریف‌ها
q: Explain the continuum fallacy and give an example.
a: It is the inference from “there is no sharp boundary between X and Y” to “there is no real difference between X and Y.” Example: “There is no precise number of drinks at which someone becomes drunk, so there’s no real difference between a sober driver and a drunk one.” Clear cases on each side differ greatly even if the boundary between them is vague.

label: فصل ۴
title: زبان، مفاهیم و تعریف‌ها
q: Identify the missing normative premise: “This factory’s emissions raise local asthma rates by 15%, so it should be shut down.”
a: Something like “Any facility whose emissions raise asthma rates by this much should be shut down.” That premise is doubtful as stated, since alternatives such as filters or relocation might be better, and the benefits of the factory must be weighed. A more defensible premise, “Facilities that cause serious avoidable health harms should be required to reduce them,” supports a weaker conclusion.

label: فصل ۴
title: زبان، مفاهیم و تعریف‌ها
q: Distinguish conceptual engineering from persuasive definition.
a: Both change the meaning of a word. Conceptual engineering does so openly, with reasons tied to the purposes the concept serves, and invites evaluation. Persuasive definition does so covertly, presenting a new meaning as the ordinary one in order to transfer the word’s emotional force.

label: فصل ۵
title: معرفت چیست؟
q: Build your own Gettier case using Zagzebski’s recipe.
a: Justified false belief: Maria checks the weather app, which says it is 20 °C; she believes it is 20 °C. The app has frozen and is showing yesterday’s data (bad luck). Good luck: today’s temperature happens also to be 20 °C. Her belief is justified and true, but she doesn’t know the temperature.

label: فصل ۵
title: معرفت چیست؟
q: Which of the theories in this chapter explains why the stopped clock case is not knowledge? Which explain the fake barn case?
a: Stopped clock: the causal theory (the time didn’t cause the reading), defeasibility (the true proposition “the clock has stopped” defeats), sensitivity (if it weren’t 2:00, he’d still believe it was), safety (he could easily have been wrong), and virtue accounts (the truth isn’t due to competence). No false lemmas arguably handles it if he implicitly believes “this clock is working.” Fake barns: reliabilism with discrimination, sensitivity, safety, and defeasibility; not no false lemmas or the causal theory; virtue accounts only with qualifications.

label: فصل ۵
title: معرفت چیست؟
q: Explain the difference between sensitivity and safety, with an example where they give different verdicts.
a: Sensitivity: in the nearest worlds where p is false, would you still believe p? Safety: in nearby worlds where you believe p, is p true? The trash chute case: if the trash hadn’t reached the basement (a remote possibility), I would still believe it had, so the belief is insensitive; but in all nearby worlds where I believe it reached the basement, it did, so it is safe. Sensitivity says I don’t know; safety says I do. The same divergence arises with “I am not a brain in a vat.”

label: فصل ۵
title: معرفت چیست؟
q: A financial pundit correctly predicted the last recession. Is this good evidence that the pundit knows how to predict recessions?
a: Not by itself. The prediction might be a Gettier-type hit: right for the wrong reasons, or right by luck. Many pundits predict recessions every year (an old joke says economists have predicted nine of the last five recessions). To judge the pundit’s knowledge, you need the full track record, including false alarms, and some check on whether the reasoning was sound. This is a question of reliability and calibration, not a single success.

label: فصل ۵
title: معرفت چیست؟
q: What is the swamping problem, and how does the achievement view answer it?
a: If reliability is valuable only as a means to true belief, then once a belief is true, its having been reliably produced adds no value (like a good espresso from a reliable machine versus the same espresso from an unreliable one). The achievement view says knowledge is a success due to ability, and such achievements have value beyond their products, just as a victory earned by skill is more valuable than the same result obtained by luck.

label: فصل ۵
title: معرفت چیست؟
q: Why does Williamson think you can know something without knowing that you know it?
a: Because knowledge requires a margin for error (safety): you know p only if you couldn’t easily have been wrong. Near the boundary of a gradually changing condition, you can be in the condition while any belief that you are in it would be unsafe, since nearby cases fall on the other side. So the condition isn’t “luminous.” Applied to knowledge itself, this means you can know p in circumstances where you are not in a position to know that you know p.

label: فصل ۵
title: معرفت چیست؟
q: Give one example each of content luck, evidential luck, and veritic luck.
a: Content luck: it’s lucky that I won the lottery, but I know I won (I checked the official results). Evidential luck: I happen to overhear a conversation revealing the surprise party; I now know about it. Veritic luck: I guess the answer to a quiz question and happen to be right; I didn’t know.

label: فصل ۵
title: معرفت چیست؟
q: How would Craig’s account of the concept of knowledge explain the lottery assertion puzzle?
a: On Craig’s view, a knower is a reliable informant about whether p. Before the draw, no one can be an informant on which ticket will lose, because they have no information discriminating this ticket from the winner. Probability alone, without discriminating information, doesn’t make someone a good informant. So we don’t treat anyone as knowing that a particular ticket will lose, and flat assertions that it will are inappropriate.

label: فصل ۶
title: توجیه: ساختار دلایل خوب
q: Distinguish propositional from doxastic justification with an example of your own.
a: Propositional: you have good reasons available for p. Doxastic: your actual belief in p is based on good reasons. Example: a juror has heard strong DNA evidence of guilt but votes guilty because the defendant “looks shifty.” She has propositional justification for the verdict, but her belief is not doxastically justified.

label: فصل ۶
title: توجیه: ساختار دلایل خوب
q: Classify each as a rebutting or undercutting defeater. You believe your friend is at home because her car is in the driveway. (a) You learn she lent her car to her brother this week. (b) You get a text from her saying she’s at the airport.
a: (a) Undercutting: it removes the support the car gave, without showing she is not at home. (b) Rebutting: it is direct evidence that she is not at home.

label: فصل ۶
title: توجیه: ساختار دلایل خوب
q: State Agrippa’s trilemma and the theory that embraces each horn.
a: Every justification ends in an infinite regress, a circle, or an unjustified assumption. Infinitism embraces the regress; coherentism embraces a (holistic) circle; foundationalism stops at “assumptions,” which it argues are non-arbitrary basic beliefs. Skepticism and critical rationalism take the trilemma to show that positive justification is unavailable.

label: فصل ۶
title: توجیه: ساختار دلایل خوب
q: What is the Sellarsian dilemma, and how do modest foundationalists reply?
a: Experience either has propositional content (and so needs justification itself) or lacks it (and so cannot logically support beliefs). Either way it cannot be a foundation. Modest foundationalists reply that experiences have propositional content but are not beliefs; they can be accurate or inaccurate, but they are not the kind of state that needs justification. They can confer justification without requiring it.

label: فصل ۶
title: توجیه: ساختار دلایل خوب
q: Why is the coherence of a conspiracy theory weak evidence of its truth?
a: Because coherence increases the probability of truth only when the cohering pieces come from independent sources. Conspiracy theories are typically built to fit: facts are selected and interpreted through the theory, anomalies are absorbed by adding auxiliary claims, and counter-evidence is reinterpreted as part of the cover-up. That kind of coherence can be manufactured for almost any story. Formal results in Bayesian epistemology confirm that coherence alone is not truth-conducive.

label: فصل ۶
title: توجیه: ساختار دلایل خوب
q: What is the new evil demon problem, and which theory does it target?
a: Your mental duplicate in a demon world has the same experiences and reasons in the same way, but all their perceptual beliefs are false and produced by unreliable processes. Intuitively, the duplicate is as justified as you are. This targets reliabilism, which implies that the duplicate is unjustified, and supports internalism.

label: فصل ۶
title: توجیه: ساختار دلایل خوب
q: Can you be blamed for a belief if you cannot choose what to believe?
a: Arguably yes. (1) You control your inquiry: what evidence you seek, what you attend to, which sources you trust. (2) On a compatibilist view, beliefs are free when they respond to reasons. (3) On Hieronymi’s view, you are answerable for your beliefs because they express your own judgment, just as you are answerable for your resentment or admiration.

label: فصل ۶
title: توجیه: ساختار دلایل خوب
q: Is “I know that vaccines don’t cause autism, but I could be wrong” coherent?
a: On a fallibilist view, yes. Knowledge does not require the impossibility of error, and the evidence against a vaccine–autism link is very strong (large studies involving millions of children, and the original 1998 paper was retracted after it was found to be fraudulent). But the sentence sounds odd, and some philosophers (Lewis) take the oddness seriously. A more natural way to express the same fallibilist stance: “The evidence is overwhelming, and I’d need extraordinary new evidence to change my mind.”

label: فصل ۷
title: منابع معرفت
q: Explain the argument from illusion and Austin’s objection to it.
a: The argument: a straight stick in water looks bent; what we see is bent; the stick is not; so what we see is not the stick but a sense-datum. Austin: we see a straight stick that looks bent; nothing bent is seen. The argument slides from “looks F” to “is an F-looking thing.” He also objected to treating illusions (misperceptions of real objects) as if they were hallucinations.

label: فصل ۷
title: منابع معرفت
q: What is the “veil of perception” problem?
a: If we perceive the world only indirectly, via mental representations, we can never compare the representations with the world itself to check that they match. So it is unclear how perception could give knowledge of the external world. The problem motivates idealism (Berkeley), skepticism, and direct realism (Reid).

label: فصل ۷
title: منابع معرفت
q: A witness says, “I’m 100% certain; I’ll never forget that face.” Six months later, she identifies the defendant with total confidence. What should a juror consider?
a: Whether her initial identification was made promptly, under fair procedures, and with high confidence (which is diagnostic); whether her confidence grew over time through feedback, repetition, or exposure to the defendant’s face (which inflates confidence without improving accuracy); the conditions of the original observation (lighting, distance, stress, duration, weapon focus); and whether the identification is cross-racial, which is known to be less accurate. Vividness and certainty today are poor indicators on their own.

label: فصل ۷
title: منابع معرفت
q: What did Nisbett and Wilson’s stocking study show?
a: People’s choices were influenced by position (they preferred the item on the right), but they didn’t mention position and denied it when asked, citing product quality instead. When people explain their own behavior, they often rely on plausible theories rather than direct introspective access to the actual causes.

label: فصل ۷
title: منابع معرفت
q: What is the difference between reductionism and anti-reductionism about testimony? Which better describes how a young child learns?
a: Reductionism: testimonial justification requires independent (non-testimonial) positive reasons to trust the speaker. Anti-reductionism: testimony is justified by default, absent defeaters. Young children learn by trusting before they could have independent evidence of reliability, which supports anti-reductionism about them, though psychological research also shows that even young children track informants’ past accuracy and prefer reliable ones (so they are not totally undiscriminating).

label: فصل ۷
title: منابع معرفت
q: Why is the creationist teacher case important?
a: It suggests that testimony can generate knowledge rather than merely transmit it. The students come to know that humans evolved, although their teacher does not believe it. What matters is that the testimony is a reliable conduit of information, not that the speaker knows.

label: فصل ۷
title: منابع معرفت
q: When is a “gut feeling” trustworthy, according to Kahneman and Klein?
a: When the environment is regular enough to be predictable and the person has had extensive practice with rapid, clear feedback. An experienced nurse’s sense that a patient is deteriorating may be reliable; a pundit’s gut feeling about next year’s election or the stock market is not.

label: فصل ۷
title: منابع معرفت
q: What does non-Euclidean geometry teach about claims of self-evidence?
a: Kant held that Euclidean geometry was necessarily and knowably true of space. Non-Euclidean geometries proved consistent, and general relativity found physical space-time to be non-Euclidean. Something that seemed self-evident and inconceivable to deny turned out false (as a claim about physical space). “It’s self-evident” should prompt examination, not end discussion.

label: فصل ۸
title: شکاکیت و پاسخ‌های آن
q: State the closure argument for skepticism and identify which premise each of these rejects: Moore, Nozick, the contextualist.
a: (1) I don’t know I’m not a BIV. (2) If I know I have hands, I know I’m not a BIV. (3) So I don’t know I have hands. Moore rejects (1): I know I have hands, so by closure I know I’m not a BIV. Nozick rejects (2): closure fails. The contextualist says the argument is sound in high-standards contexts and (1) is false in ordinary ones, so the conclusion doesn’t threaten ordinary knowledge claims.

label: فصل ۸
title: شکاکیت و پاسخ‌های آن
q: How does the Pyrrhonist answer the charge that one cannot live without beliefs?
a: The Pyrrhonist lives by appearances, following nature, feelings, customs, and skills, without asserting that things really are as they appear. He eats because he is hungry and food appears nourishing, not because he dogmatically believes food nourishes.

label: فصل ۸
title: شکاکیت و پاسخ‌های آن
q: Explain DeRose’s bank cases. How does contextualism explain them? How does subject-sensitive invariantism explain them differently?
a: In the low-stakes case, “I know the bank will be open tomorrow” seems true; in the high-stakes case, with the same evidence, “I don’t know” seems true. Contextualism: the attributor’s context raises the standards for “know” in the high-stakes case, so the sentence expresses a different proposition. Subject-sensitive invariantism: “know” means the same, but whether the subject knows depends on the subject’s stakes, so Keith actually knows in Case A and doesn’t know in Case B.

label: فصل ۸
title: شکاکیت و پاسخ‌های آن
q: What is Putnam’s argument that we are not brains in vats, and what is one limitation?
a: By semantic externalism, a lifelong BIV’s word “vat” refers to simulated vats, so its thought “I am a BIV” is false; if I’m not a BIV, the thought is also false; so it is false either way. Limitation: it doesn’t apply to a recently envatted brain, whose words still refer to real vats. It also may not rule out other skeptical scenarios.

label: فصل ۸
title: شکاکیت و پاسخ‌های آن
q: What is the “easy knowledge” problem for dogmatism?
a: If a perceptual experience of p immediately justifies p without prior justification that one’s perception is working, then one can use perceptions to justify beliefs that one’s perception is not being fooled. (The table looks red, so it’s red, so it’s not a white table under red light.) Or one can bootstrap a source’s reliability from its own outputs (Vogel’s gas gauge). This seems illegitimately easy.

label: فصل ۸
title: شکاکیت و پاسخ‌های آن
q: A commentator says, “You can’t prove that the new medicine is completely safe, so it’s reckless to approve it.” Using this chapter, diagnose the argument.
a: It demands certainty (impossible expectations / nirvana fallacy) and implicitly relies on infallibilism: if knowledge or justified action required ruling out every possibility of harm, no medicine, food, or activity could ever be approved. The relevant question is comparative: how strong is the evidence of safety and benefit, relative to the risks of the alternatives (including not treating)? The argument also fails the consequences test: applied consistently, it would condemn the treatments the commentator already accepts.

label: فصل ۸
title: شکاکیت و پاسخ‌های آن
q: How does hinge epistemology respond to the skeptic, and what is one worry about it?
a: It holds that certain propositions (such as “I have hands” or “the world has existed for a long time”) are not conclusions from evidence but the framework that makes evidence and doubt possible; doubting them is not a coherent move in the practice of giving reasons. Worries: it seems to concede that we don’t know the hinges; and if different communities have different hinges, it may lead to relativism and to deep disagreements that reason cannot resolve.

label: فصل ۸
title: شکاکیت و پاسخ‌های آن
q: Why is Bostrom’s simulation argument different from the brain-in-a-vat argument?
a: The BIV argument relies on the mere possibility of an undetectable scenario and concludes we lack knowledge. Bostrom’s argument is probabilistic and disjunctive: it concludes that at least one of three claims is true, and only one of them is that we are probably simulated. Also, following Chalmers, being in a simulation might not make most of our beliefs false.

label: فصل ۹
title: استقرا، احتمال و استدلال بیزی
q: State Hume’s problem of induction in three steps.
a: (1) Inductive inference presupposes that the unobserved resembles the observed. (2) This can’t be proven a priori, since its denial is conceivable. (3) It can’t be proven from experience without circularity. So induction has no rational foundation.

label: فصل ۹
title: استقرا، احتمال و استدلال بیزی
q: Explain why “grue” poses a problem even for someone who accepts induction.
a: The same evidence (all emeralds examined so far are green, and therefore grue) supports incompatible generalizations. Induction alone can’t tell us which predicate to project. We need an account of which categories are “projectible,” and that account can’t be read off the evidence.

label: فصل ۹
title: استقرا، احتمال و استدلال بیزی
q: A test for a rare disease (prevalence 1 in 1,000) has sensitivity 99% and a false positive rate of 2%. You test positive. Roughly how likely are you to have the disease? Use natural frequencies.
a: Of 100,000 people, 100 have the disease and 99 test positive. Of 99,900 who don’t, 2% (1,998) test positive. So 99 of about 2,097 positives have the disease: about 4.7%. A positive result raises the probability almost fifty-fold, but it is still more likely that you don’t have the disease. A second, independent test would help a lot (likelihood ratio 0.99/0.02 ≈ 50 each time).

label: فصل ۹
title: استقرا، احتمال و استدلال بیزی
q: What is the likelihood ratio of a piece of evidence that is “consistent with” a hypothesis but equally consistent with its negation?
a: 1. It provides no evidence either way, however well it “fits.”

label: فصل ۹
title: استقرا، احتمال و استدلال بیزی
q: Why is a vivid, detailed scenario often less probable than a plain one?
a: Because each added detail is an extra conjunct, and P(A and B) ≤ P(A). Detail increases representativeness and plausibility, which makes the story feel more likely, while its probability can only fall.

label: فصل ۹
title: استقرا، احتمال و استدلال بیزی
q: A school introduces a new program for its lowest-scoring students, and next year their scores rise. What alternative explanation should you consider first?
a: Regression to the mean. Students selected for extremely low scores partly had bad luck on the test; on average, their next scores will be closer to the mean regardless of the program. A comparison group of similarly selected students without the program is needed.

label: فصل ۹
title: استقرا، احتمال و استدلال بیزی
q: A newspaper reports: “Eating processed meat increases your risk of bowel cancer by 18%.” What should you ask?
a: “From what, to what?” An 18% relative increase in a lifetime risk of, say, 5 or 6% amounts to an absolute increase of about 1 percentage point. You would also ask how much meat was involved, whether the association is causal (observational data, possible confounding), and what the uncertainty is. (For reference: the International Agency for Research on Cancer reported an 18% increased risk per 50 g of processed meat eaten daily.)

label: فصل ۹
title: استقرا، احتمال و استدلال بیزی
q: In Simpson’s paradox, how do you decide whether to trust the aggregated or the separated data?
a: By the causal structure. If the grouping variable (e.g., stone size) is a common cause of both the treatment choice and the outcome, compare within groups. If the grouping variable is itself caused by the treatment (a mediator), the aggregate may be the right comparison. Statistics alone can’t decide; you need a causal model.

label: فصل ۹
title: استقرا، احتمال و استدلال بیزی
q: Why does Cromwell’s rule matter for open-mindedness?
a: Because a prior of exactly 0 or 1 can never be changed by any evidence under Bayesian updating. To remain responsive to evidence, you must leave at least some probability for being wrong. A belief held with literal certainty is immune to evidence, which is the formal definition of a closed mind.

label: فصل ۱۰
title: علم، شواهد و تبیین
q: Explain the asymmetry between verification and falsification, and why it isn’t the whole story.
a: No number of confirming instances proves a universal law, but one counterexample logically refutes it. It isn’t the whole story because of the Duhem–Quine problem: predictions depend on auxiliary assumptions, so a failed prediction may refute an auxiliary rather than the theory. Also, probabilistic and existential hypotheses aren’t strictly falsifiable, and scientists reasonably retain theories in the face of some anomalies.

label: فصل ۱۰
title: علم، شواهد و تبیین
q: When Uranus’s orbit didn’t match Newtonian predictions, astronomers postulated a new planet. Was this ad hoc? Why or why not?
a: No. The hypothesis was independently testable: it predicted a planet of a certain mass at a certain position, which could be looked for, and it was found (Neptune, 1846). An ad hoc hypothesis has no consequences beyond saving the theory.

label: فصل ۱۰
title: علم، شواهد و تبیین
q: What distinguishes a progressive from a degenerating research programme?
a: A progressive programme’s modifications predict novel facts, some of which are confirmed. A degenerating programme’s modifications only accommodate known facts after the event, and its predictions fail or lag behind the evidence.

label: فصل ۱۰
title: علم، شواهد و تبیین
q: “Children who eat breakfast do better at school, so schools should provide breakfast to improve grades.” Give three alternative explanations for the correlation.
a: (1) Confounding: families with more resources and stability both provide breakfast and support schoolwork. (2) Confounding by health or sleep: well-rested, healthy children are more likely to eat breakfast and to concentrate. (3) Reverse causation or selection: motivated, organized children may be more likely to get up in time for breakfast. The claim may still be true (and there is some experimental evidence on school breakfast programs), but the correlation alone doesn’t establish it.

label: فصل ۱۰
title: علم، شواهد و تبیین
q: Why does randomization matter in a controlled trial?
a: It makes the treatment and control groups similar, on average, in all respects, including factors nobody thought to measure. This breaks any systematic link between the treatment and confounders, so differences in outcome can be attributed to the treatment (up to chance, which statistics can quantify).

label: فصل ۱۰
title: علم، شواهد و تبیین
q: What are the no-miracles argument and the pessimistic meta-induction?
a: No-miracles: the success of science would be a miracle unless our theories were approximately true, so they probably are. Pessimistic meta-induction: many past successful theories were false (phlogiston, ether, caloric), so our current successful theories are probably false too. Structural realism and selective realism try to accommodate both.

label: فصل ۱۰
title: علم، شواهد و تبیین
q: Someone says: “Scientists were wrong about ulcers and continental drift, so I don’t trust the scientific consensus on vaccines.” Evaluate.
a: The premise is true, but the conclusion doesn’t follow. Consensus is sometimes overturned, but much less often than it is confirmed; the base rate matters. The corrections came from new evidence within science, not from rejecting science. The consensus on vaccine safety rests on many independent lines of evidence (large observational studies of millions, trials, surveillance systems in many countries). The appropriate response to fallibility is to follow the evidence, which here strongly supports the consensus, not to reject it wholesale. There is also an asymmetry test: would the speaker apply the same reasoning to reject consensus claims they like?

label: فصل ۱۰
title: علم، شواهد و تبیین
q: Why is the Forer effect relevant to evaluating personality tests, astrology, and “cold reading” by psychics?
a: Because vague, general, and double-sided descriptions feel personally accurate to almost everyone. A subjective sense of “that’s so me” is therefore no evidence that the method has any real diagnostic power. The proper test is whether people can pick out their own description from others’ better than chance, under blind conditions.

label: فصل ۱۱
title: حقیقت، نسبی‌گرایی و عینیت
q: State the T-schema and explain how it bears on the claim that “truth is relative.”
a: “p” is true if and only if p. For example, “Water boils at 100 °C at sea level” is true if and only if water boils at 100 °C at sea level. So the truth of the sentence depends on how things are with water, not on who believes it. If truth were relative to believers, the T-schema would fail, since the sentence could be “true for” someone while water did not boil at that temperature.

label: فصل ۱۱
title: حقیقت، نسبی‌گرایی و عینیت
q: What is the main objection to the coherence theory of truth?
a: There can be many internally coherent but mutually incompatible systems (a consistent novel, a consistent set of false beliefs), so coherence alone can’t be what truth is. The theory seems to confuse a test of justification with the nature of truth.

label: فصل ۱۱
title: حقیقت، نسبی‌گرایی و عینیت
q: How does deflationism explain the usefulness of the word “true,” if truth has no substantial nature?
a: “True” is a logical device for generalization and endorsement without repetition: “Everything she said is true,” “The theorem is true,” “Always tell the truth.” These can’t easily be expressed without a truth predicate, since we can’t list all the propositions involved.

label: فصل ۱۱
title: حقیقت، نسبی‌گرایی و عینیت
q: Reconstruct the self-refutation argument against global truth relativism.
a: “All truth is relative” is either absolutely true or relatively true. If absolutely true, there is at least one absolute truth, so the claim is false. If only relatively true (true for relativists), it may be false for non-relativists, and the relativist has no non-relative ground to ask them to accept it. Either way the global thesis fails.

label: فصل ۱۱
title: حقیقت، نسبی‌گرایی و عینیت
q: “Different cultures have different moral beliefs, so there is no objective morality.” Evaluate.
a: The premise (descriptive relativism) is true, but the conclusion doesn’t follow. Different cultures also had different beliefs about the shape of the Earth and the causes of disease, without showing there is no fact about those things. Disagreement is compatible with one view being right. Also, much apparent moral disagreement reflects different factual beliefs (for example, about the afterlife or about the effects of a practice) combined with shared values. Moral objectivity may still be false, but this argument doesn’t show it.

label: فصل ۱۱
title: حقیقت، نسبی‌گرایی و عینیت
q: What is the difference between lying and bullshit, according to Frankfurt?
a: The liar knows the truth and tries to lead others away from it; the liar is still oriented toward truth. The bullshitter is indifferent to whether what they say is true; they are pursuing some other goal (impressing, persuading, filling space). Frankfurt thinks bullshit is more corrosive because it abandons the practice of caring about truth.

label: فصل ۱۱
title: حقیقت، نسبی‌گرایی و عینیت
q: Distinguish perspectivism from relativism.
a: Perspectivism holds that knowledge is always from some perspective and that combining more perspectives gives a more complete (more objective) understanding of a single reality. Relativism holds that truth itself varies with perspective, with no single reality that all perspectives are about. The blind men and the elephant illustrate perspectivism: there is one elephant.

label: فصل ۱۱
title: حقیقت، نسبی‌گرایی و عینیت
q: Give an example of a socially constructed fact that is nonetheless objective in the sense that your believing otherwise doesn’t change it.
a: The fact that you owe your bank 5,000 euros. Money, debts, and banks exist only because of collective human practices (they are institutional facts). But given those practices, the debt is real whether or not you believe in it.

label: فصل ۱۲
title: معرفت‌شناسی اجتماعی: باهم دانستن
q: What is Hardwig’s argument that rational belief often requires deference?
a: Modern knowledge is produced by divisions of cognitive labor so extensive that no individual can check more than a tiny part of it; even the authors of a scientific paper rely on each other. So a rational layperson who refused to believe anything they couldn’t personally verify would believe almost nothing. Rationality requires trusting reliable others.

label: فصل ۱۲
title: معرفت‌شناسی اجتماعی: باهم دانستن
q: A novice must choose between two doctors who disagree. List three of Goldman’s sources of evidence she could use.
a: Any three of: (A) which doctor responds better to the other’s arguments; (B) how many other independent doctors agree with each; (C) credentials and professional standing; (D) conflicts of interest or biases; (E) past track records, including checkable predictions.

label: فصل ۱۲
title: معرفت‌شناسی اجتماعی: باهم دانستن
q: Why is agreement among many people weak evidence when their beliefs are not independent?
a: Because if people are copying each other (following a leader, joining a cascade, repeating the same source), their agreement contains little more information than the original source. Independent agreement is strong evidence because it would be unlikely if the claim were false; dependent agreement is what you would expect whether or not it is true.

label: فصل ۱۲
title: معرفت‌شناسی اجتماعی: باهم دانستن
q: Explain the restaurant bill case and what conciliationists and steadfasters say about it.
a: You calculate your share as $43; an equally competent friend with the same information gets $45. Conciliationists say you should significantly lower your confidence, since you have no independent reason to think you, rather than your friend, made the error. Most steadfasters agree in this case, because the disagreement is evidence of a calculation error somewhere; the dispute is about harder cases (politics, philosophy) where the parties have reflected at length.

label: فصل ۱۲
title: معرفت‌شناسی اجتماعی: باهم دانستن
q: Distinguish testimonial from hermeneutical injustice, with an example of each.
a: Testimonial injustice: a speaker is given less credibility than deserved because of identity prejudice (e.g., a patient’s report of pain discounted because of their race). Hermeneutical injustice: a gap in shared concepts leaves someone unable to understand or communicate their experience because their group was excluded from shaping those concepts (e.g., experiences of sexual harassment before the concept existed).

label: فصل ۱۲
title: معرفت‌شناسی اجتماعی: باهم دانستن
q: What’s the difference between an epistemic bubble and an echo chamber? Why does it matter?
a: A bubble omits other voices; an echo chamber actively discredits them by manipulating trust. Bubbles can be burst by exposure to other views; echo chambers are strengthened by exposure, since members have been prepared to reject outsiders. Addressing an echo chamber requires rebuilding trust, not just supplying information.

label: فصل ۱۲
title: معرفت‌شناسی اجتماعی: باهم دانستن
q: Why did the crowd’s estimate of the ox’s weight work so well, and when would it fail?
a: The guesses were diverse and independent, so individual errors in different directions largely canceled out when aggregated (by the median). It would fail if people’s guesses were influenced by each other (reducing independence), or if most people shared the same systematic bias.

label: فصل ۱۲
title: معرفت‌شناسی اجتماعی: باهم دانستن
q: Apply Keeley’s criteria to the claim that “the 1969 moon landing was faked.”
a: It relies on errant data (flag “waving,” missing stars in photos), each of which has a mundane explanation. It is self-sealing (evidence such as retroreflectors left on the Moon, independent tracking of the missions by other countries including the Soviet Union, and returned samples are dismissed as part of the fake). It requires an enormous number of conspirators (hundreds of thousands) to keep a secret for decades, including a geopolitical rival with every incentive to expose it. And it requires the conspirators to be capable of faking everything perfectly yet careless enough to leave “clues.”

label: فصل ۱۳
title: فضیلت فکری و اخلاق باور
q: Why does Clifford say the shipowner is guilty even if the ship arrives safely?
a: Because the wrong lay in how he formed his belief (stifling his doubts rather than investigating), not in its consequences. Luck in the outcome doesn’t change the wrongness of the process: “he would not have been innocent, he would only have been not found out.”

label: فصل ۱۳
title: فضیلت فکری و اخلاق باور
q: State James’s conditions for a “genuine option.” Give an example of a genuine option and of one that isn’t.
a: Live (both options are real possibilities for you), forced (no third alternative), and momentous (unique, high stakes, irreversible). For James, and for many people, the choice whether to have religious faith. Not genuine: whether to believe that a particular stock will rise (avoidable, since you can suspend judgment and not invest, and not momentous for most).

label: فصل ۱۳
title: فضیلت فکری و اخلاق باور
q: Distinguish reliabilist and responsibilist virtue epistemology.
a: Reliabilists take intellectual virtues to be reliable cognitive faculties (good vision, memory, reasoning). Responsibilists take them to be character traits (open-mindedness, intellectual courage, humility) involving motivation to know as well as skill.

label: فصل ۱۳
title: فضیلت فکری و اخلاق باور
q: Give the vices of deficiency and excess for intellectual tenacity and for open-mindedness.
a: Tenacity: giving up too easily (deficiency), stubbornness or dogmatism (excess). Open-mindedness: closed-mindedness (deficiency), credulity or indecision (excess).

label: فصل ۱۳
title: فضیلت فکری و اخلاق باور
q: What is a “stealthy” vice, and what follows for how we should guard against vices?
a: A vice that tends to hide itself from the person who has it, because it impairs the very capacities needed to detect it (closed-mindedness closes one to evidence of closed-mindedness). So we can’t rely on introspection to catch our own vices; we need external checks: feedback from others, structured habits (like Darwin’s golden rule), and institutions that expose our reasoning to criticism.

label: فصل ۱۳
title: فضیلت فکری و اخلاق باور
q: Is it closed-minded to refuse to change your mind in response to an argument you can’t refute?
a: Not necessarily. If you have overwhelming independent evidence that the conclusion is false (as with Zeno’s arguments against motion), you can reasonably conclude that the argument has a flaw you haven’t found. But this is only reasonable when your independent evidence really is overwhelming. Using the same move to protect weakly supported beliefs is closed-mindedness.

label: فصل ۱۳
title: فضیلت فکری و اخلاق باور
q: Explain Flew’s gardener parable and one reply to it.
a: The believer’s claim about a gardener is qualified each time evidence fails to support it, until it becomes indistinguishable from the claim that there is no gardener. Flew concluded that such claims “die the death of a thousand qualifications.” Replies: Hare’s “bliks” (religious beliefs are interpretive frameworks, not hypotheses); Mitchell’s partisan (evidence can count against a belief held on trust, without the believer abandoning it, as with trust in a person).

label: فصل ۱۳
title: فضیلت فکری و اخلاق باور
q: What practical principle follows from the pragmatic encroachment debate, whichever side is right?
a: When the cost of error is high, gather more evidence and be more cautious before acting. The debate is about whether this is a fact about knowledge itself or about practical rationality, but the practical advice is the same.

label: فصل ۱۴
title: روان‌شناسی استدلال: ذهن در عمل
q: Explain why the intuitive answer to the bat-and-ball problem is wrong, and what the problem measures.
a: If the ball cost 10 cents, the bat would cost $1.10 and the total $1.20. The correct answer is 5 cents (ball) and $1.05 (bat). The problem measures cognitive reflection: the tendency to notice that an immediate, intuitive answer needs checking, and to check it.

label: فصل ۱۴
title: روان‌شناسی استدلال: ذهن در عمل
q: Two groups receive the same information about a medical treatment, one framed in survival rates and one in mortality rates, and choose differently. What does this show, and how can you protect yourself?
a: A framing effect: logically equivalent descriptions produce different choices. Protect yourself by restating the options in the opposite frame, and in absolute numbers, and checking whether your preference changes.

label: فصل ۱۴
title: روان‌شناسی استدلال: ذهن در عمل
q: In the Wason selection task (E, K, 4, 7; rule: “if vowel, then even”), why is turning over the 4 useless?
a: The rule says nothing about what must be behind an even number. Whatever is behind the 4 (vowel or consonant) is consistent with the rule. Only a vowel with an odd number could falsify it, so you must check E (for an odd number) and 7 (for a vowel).

label: فصل ۱۴
title: روان‌شناسی استدلال: ذهن در عمل
q: What does Stanovich mean by saying myside bias is not reduced by intelligence? What protects against it?
a: People of higher cognitive ability show about as much myside bias as others; they are just better at producing arguments for their own side (as Perkins found with education). What helps is not ability but dispositions and methods: actively open-minded thinking, deliberately seeking the strongest opposing arguments, considering the opposite, and exposing one’s reasoning to critics.

label: فصل ۱۴
title: روان‌شناسی استدلال: ذهن در عمل
q: What is the “illusion of explanatory depth,” and how can it be used in a heated discussion?
a: People believe they understand how things work far better than they do, until they try to explain the mechanism step by step. In a discussion, asking each person (including yourself) to explain how a policy would produce its claimed effects often reveals gaps in understanding and tends to moderate extreme positions, whereas asking for reasons does not.

label: فصل ۱۴
title: روان‌شناسی استدلال: ذهن در عمل
q: Summarize the critique of the Dunning-Kruger effect.
a: Much of the classic pattern follows statistically from two facts: self-assessments correlate only weakly with actual performance, and most people rate themselves above average. Together these guarantee that low performers overestimate and high performers underestimate, even with no special metacognitive deficit among the unskilled. What survives is that people are generally poor judges of their own competence. The popular claim that incompetent people think they’re experts is not supported.

label: فصل ۱۴
title: روان‌شناسی استدلال: ذهن در عمل
q: According to the argumentative theory, why do groups outperform individuals on the Wason selection task?
a: Because reasoning is better at evaluating others’ arguments than at producing unbiased arguments of one’s own. In a group, a correct argument, once someone produces it, is recognized as correct by others, and weak arguments are criticized. Individuals, reasoning alone, tend to accept their own first intuitions and weak justifications.

label: فصل ۱۴
title: روان‌شناسی استدلال: ذهن در عمل
q: Why is “be unbiased” a poor debiasing instruction, and what works better?
a: Because people don’t perceive their own bias (the bias blind spot), so they believe they are already unbiased. Specific procedures work better: considering what you would think if the same evidence pointed the other way, generating alternative explanations, premortems, base rates, checklists, blind analysis, and structured group deliberation.

label: فصل ۱۵
title: راهنمای میدانی مغالطه‌ها
q: “The mayor says the new bike lanes have reduced accidents, but he’s a cyclist himself, so of course he’d say that.”
a: Circumstantial ad hominem. His interest is a reason to check the accident data, not a reason to dismiss his claim.

label: فصل ۱۵
title: راهنمای میدانی مغالطه‌ها
q: “We can’t ban plastic bags. What’s next, banning plastic bottles, then plastic toys, then all plastic? We’ll be back in the Stone Age.”
a: Slippery slope, without a mechanism or evidence for the steps, ending in hyperbole. Each step would need a separate argument.

label: فصل ۱۵
title: راهنمای میدانی مغالطه‌ها
q: “Thousands of people have been helped by crystal healing. Just read the testimonials.”
a: Appeal to popularity and anecdotal evidence (hasty generalization), with survivorship bias (we hear from satisfied customers), and possible post hoc reasoning (people improve for other reasons).

label: فصل ۱۵
title: راهنمای میدانی مغالطه‌ها
q: “Either you support this surveillance program, or you don’t care about stopping terrorism.”
a: False dilemma. One can care about stopping terrorism and oppose this particular program (e.g., believing it ineffective or too costly to privacy).

label: فصل ۱۵
title: راهنمای میدانی مغالطه‌ها
q: “Nobody has ever shown that this food additive is harmful, so it’s perfectly safe.”
a: Argument from ignorance, unless it has been well tested. If thorough safety studies have been done and found nothing, the absence of evidence of harm is genuine evidence of safety (the legitimate cousin). The key question is whether it has been properly studied.

label: فصل ۱۵
title: راهنمای میدانی مغالطه‌ها
q: “My opponent says we should consider raising taxes on the highest earners. So he wants to punish success and destroy the economy.”
a: Straw man (and loaded language: “punish success”). The actual proposal was to consider a tax increase on one group.

label: فصل ۱۵
title: راهنمای میدانی مغالطه‌ها
q: “Ninety-seven percent of climate scientists agree that recent warming is mainly human-caused, so we have strong reason to believe it is.”
a: Not a fallacy: a legitimate appeal to expert consensus in the relevant field. (It would still be worth knowing what the evidence is, but the consensus is itself strong evidence for a non-expert.)

label: فصل ۱۵
title: راهنمای میدانی مغالطه‌ها
q: “I’ve had three flights delayed with this airline. It’s the worst airline in the world.”
a: Hasty generalization from a tiny sample, with no comparison to other airlines’ delay rates.

label: فصل ۱۵
title: راهنمای میدانی مغالطه‌ها
q: “Critics say our program didn’t reduce homelessness. But the critics don’t understand that real success can’t be measured by numbers.”
a: Possibly moving the goalposts or a motte-and-bailey retreat: the program was presumably promoted as reducing homelessness, a measurable outcome. If success “can’t be measured,” the claim becomes unfalsifiable. (It’s legitimate to argue for additional measures of success, but not to abandon the original claim when it fails.)

label: فصل ۱۵
title: راهنمای میدانی مغالطه‌ها
q: “Each ingredient in this cake is delicious, so the cake must be delicious.”
a: Composition. Garlic, chocolate, and anchovies may each be delicious.

label: فصل ۱۵
title: راهنمای میدانی مغالطه‌ها
q: “After the city introduced the curfew for teenagers, juvenile crime fell by 10%. The curfew works.”
a: Post hoc. Was crime falling anyway, elsewhere too? Was the curfew introduced after an unusually bad year (regression to the mean)? A comparison with similar cities without curfews is needed.

label: فصل ۱۵
title: راهنمای میدانی مغالطه‌ها
q: “You can’t trust the study showing that the drug works; it was funded by the manufacturer. So the drug doesn’t work.”
a: The first part is a legitimate reason for caution (conflicts of interest are associated with favorable results), but the conclusion commits the fallacy fallacy combined with ad hominem: the study’s funding doesn’t show the drug doesn’t work. The right conclusion is “we need independent evidence.”

label: فصل ۱۵
title: راهنمای میدانی مغالطه‌ها
q: “A: No scientist accepts astrology. B: What about Dr. Smith? She’s a physicist and she believes in it. A: Well, no real scientist accepts astrology.”
a: No true Scotsman. (A better reply: “Some scientists hold unusual views outside their field; what matters is the evidence, and controlled tests of astrology have found no effect.”)

label: فصل ۱۵
title: راهنمای میدانی مغالطه‌ها
q: “We’ve invested five years and a huge amount of money in this research direction. Abandoning it now would waste all of that.”
a: Sunk cost reasoning. The question is whether continuing is the best use of future resources. (The past investment may be relevant as evidence about the likelihood of success, or about what has been learned.)

label: فصل ۱۵
title: راهنمای میدانی مغالطه‌ها
q: “Why are the media ignoring the obvious connection between the new cell towers and the outbreak of headaches in our town?”
a: Loaded question (presupposes an “obvious connection” and that the media are “ignoring” it), and likely post hoc / Texas sharpshooter (headaches are common; noticing them after the towers went up is expected). The questions to ask: what’s the evidence of a connection, and what are the base rates of headaches before and after?
